query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At 400–700 °C the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by how quickly a dense, adherent Cr- and Ni-rich spinel tribo-oxide glaze can form; a very fine initial grain size (< 30 nm) promotes this by providing high grain-boundary diffusion paths. Therefore, coatings with an ultrafine grain structure will show significantly lower high-temperature wear than otherwise identical, coarse-grained coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: Magnetron-sputtered FeNiCrCoCu coating, 3 µm thick, on hardened steel substrate; FCC solid-solution with random texture and average grain size ≈100 nm (baseline).
generation.intervention: Increase sputter power and apply −100 V substrate bias to obtain an ultrafine grain structure (~15 nm) while keeping chemistry and thickness unchanged.
generation.conditions: Pin-on-disk wear against an alumina ball, 5 N normal load, 0.1 m s⁻¹ sliding speed, dry air at 400, 600 and 700 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: High density of grain boundaries that accelerate outward diffusion of Cr and Ni, forming a continuous Cr–Ni spinel oxide layer during the first few sliding passes.
generation.mechanism: Rapid tribo-oxidation on the ultrafine-grained surface yields an adherent, lubricious glaze that suppresses metal–metal contact and limits third-body abrasive debris. In the coarse-grained coating, slower diffusion produces discontinuous oxides that spall, leading to higher wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Across 400–700 °C the ultrafine-grained coating will show (i) coefficient of friction 0.35–0.45 versus 0.55–0.65 for the baseline, (ii) a specific wear rate at least two-fold lower (≤1 × 10⁻⁵ mm³ N⁻¹ m⁻¹ vs ≥2 × 10⁻⁵ mm³ N⁻¹ m⁻¹) and (iii) a continuous ~100 nm thick Cr–Ni spinel layer in cross-section TEM after testing.
generation.baseline: Same coating chemistry and thickness with ~100 nm grains produced at lower sputter power and no substrate bias.
generation.boundary: Temperatures 400–700 °C and normal loads up to 15 N; outside this range (≥750 °C or ≥20 N) oxide spallation or substrate softening is expected to dominate, so the hypothesis may no longer apply.
generation.uncertainty: No published data were found that directly couple FeNiCrCoCu grain size with high-temperature wear; the magnitude of the expected wear-rate reduction is therefore approximate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two coating sets (baseline and ultrafine). Conduct identical pin-on-disk tests at 400, 600 and 700 °C. Characterise post-test surfaces by SEM/EDS, XRD and cross-section TEM to identify oxide chemistry and continuity.
measurements: Coefficient of friction vs sliding distance
Surface and cross-section oxide morphology and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If at any tested temperature the ultrafine-grained coating does NOT (a) form a noticeably more continuous Cr/Ni-rich spinel layer OR (b) achieve a ≥30 % reduction in wear rate relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
